analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Ancillary study** of NRG/RTOG 0815, a phase 3 randomized trial of dose-escalated RT with or without 6 months of STAD. Prespecified analysis plan with NCI approval, GC data linked to updated outcomes at **10.2 years** median follow-up (IQR 8.4-11.4).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Intermediate-risk prostate cancer**. GC scores were obtained for **395 pts** of 856 with available tissue, with baseline characteristics balanced between arms. GC distribution: low (<0.45) **44%**, intermediate (0.45-0.6) 24%, high (>0.6) **32%**.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: **6 months of STAD** added to dose-escalated RT vs RT alone. Agents not stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **Dose-escalated RT** in both arms. Dose, fractionation, modality mix and target volume are not stated in source, though RT modality was a covariate in the multivariable models.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** distant metastasis. **Secondary:** biochemical failure, MFS, PCSM, OS. Cox and Fine-Gray competing risk MVA adjusted for age, race, clinical risk factors, comorbidity score and RT modality.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **GC-STAD interaction for DM p<0.001** and for PCSM p-interaction <0.001. 10-yr DM absolute difference **1%** in low GC vs absolute benefit **11%** in high GC. Slide 2 shows predicted 10-yr DM rising with GC score after RT alone and staying low with RT + STAD.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The parent NRG/RTOG 0815 trial set the question of STAD with dose-escalated RT for intermediate-risk disease as a whole. Decipher has prior ancillary validation in NRG/RTOG 0126 and 9601. This analysis adds a treatment interaction inside a trial that randomized the therapy in question.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents intermediate-risk prostate cancer treated with dose-escalated RT with biopsy tissue yielding a Decipher GC score. Does not represent pts outside intermediate-risk disease or settings where RT dose and technique differ from the trial's, which the source does not specify.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The slide and the abstract cut the cohort differently (**int/high GC pooled at 8%** vs **high GC at 11%**), leaving the GC 0.45-0.6 group unresolved. The prognostic DM estimate has a CI of **0.98-24.3**. No favorable vs unfavorable intermediate-risk breakdown in source.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The predictive claim is for DM and PCSM, not OS or MFS, for which no interaction is reported in source. The low-GC finding is the clinically usable half, since it identifies a large group with **no clear benefit** from intensification. The authors themselves defer to **NRG GU010** for prospective validation.

studies.interpretation:
A biomarker earns the word predictive only when it is tested inside a trial that randomized the treatment it claims to select for, and that is what distinguishes this analysis from most of the Decipher literature. The classifier has been shown repeatedly to sort pts by prognosis, including in earlier NRG ancillary projects such as RTOG 0126 and RTOG 9601. Prognosis alone does not tell a radiation oncologist whether ADT helps a given man. Here the therapy in question, 6 months of STAD on top of dose-escalated RT, was assigned by randomization, the analysis plan was prespecified and approved by the NCI before the assay was run, and the assay was locked. Those three features are the reason to take the interaction seriously rather than file it with exploratory subgroup work.

The reasons for restraint are equally specific. The interaction for distant metastasis rests on 16 events, and the one for prostate cancer-specific mortality on 7. A p-interaction below 0.001 on that base says the pattern is unlikely to be noise within this dataset, but it does not make the size of the benefit in each stratum precise, and the source gives no confidence intervals around the 11% and 1% figures. The prognostic estimate for DM shows the same fragility, with an interval running from 0.98 to 24.3. GC scores came from 395 pts of 856 with available tissue, so the analyzed group is a subset defined by tissue availability and assay success. Arms were balanced within it, which protects the randomized comparison, but whether the subset resembles the full trial population is not something the abstract lets a reader check.

There is also an unresolved seam between the two sources. The abstract contrasts low GC with high GC, 1% against 11%. The slide contrasts low GC with intermediate and high pooled, 1% against 8%. Both can be true, and together they imply the intermediate GC group dilutes the benefit, yet neither source reports that group by itself. For a clinician the threshold matters: the decision at GC 0.5 is exactly the one the data leave open.

The asymmetry of the two findings should shape how they are used. The low-GC result is the more actionable, because it describes a large fraction of the cohort (44%) whose long-term metastasis risk was low with RT alone, and where the cost of being wrong is small in absolute terms. The high-GC result argues against omission more than it defines a new intensified standard, since 6 months of STAD was already an accepted option in this risk group. What the analysis does not show is an interaction for OS or MFS, and with 134 deaths against 16 metastases, most mortality in this population is clearly not driven by prostate cancer.

Transfer to current practice carries one more caveat. The source specifies only that RT was dose-escalated, without dose, fractionation or target volume, and does not separate favorable from unfavorable intermediate-risk disease, where baseline STAD practice already differs. NRG GU010, which the authors name as the prospective validation, is the place those questions get a randomized answer.

Phase, prespecification of this analysis and median follow-up are not stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Parent trial eligibility per slide: **post-RP, PSA 0.1-2.0 ng/mL, pT2 or pT3 N0M0, Gleason ≤9**. Of 1039 consented pts with samples, 3 had insufficient RNA, 120 failed cDNA QC and 207 failed microarray QC.

analysis_sections.body: Arm 1 **PBRT alone** (n=215), Arm 2 **PBRT + STADT** (n=247), Arm 3 **PBRT + STADT + PLNRT** (n=247). Dose, fractionation, pelvic nodal volume and STADT duration are not reported in source tweets.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Reported: **FFP** at 5 y and **MFS** at 10 y, each tested for subtype-by-treatment interaction. The primary endpoint of this biomarker analysis is not stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Tweet: 5-y FFP benefit from postop ADT **31% vs 10% (p-int=.01)** and 10-y MFS **20% vs -3% (p-int=.05)**. FFP slide: pooled STADT arms vs PBRT alone **HR 0.34 (0.23-0.52), p<0.001** in one subtype panel; the other panel's HR is garbled in OCR with CI 0.43-1.00.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The parent trial (Pollack et al, Lancet Onc 2022) is the slide's stated reference for the unselected result. GETUG-AFU 16 and RADICALS-HD tested ADT with post-RP RT without molecular selection, and NRG GU006 used PAM50 subtype prospectively with salvage RT; none of their figures appear in source.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents men post-RP with PSA 0.1-2.0 ng/mL, pT2 or pT3 N0M0, Gleason ≤9 receiving salvage RT with tissue passing PAM50 assay QC. Does not represent node-positive disease, PSA above 2.0 ng/mL, or adjuvant RT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Subtype panel labels and one HR are **not legible in OCR**, so effect sizes by subtype rest partly on the tweet's framing. The MFS interaction sits at **p-int=.05**. No multiplicity handling, event counts or Luminal B prevalence in source.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: A treatment-by-subtype interaction on FFP is the claim that would let PAM50 select for ADT; a prognostic signal alone would not. The MFS interaction is weaker and the three-arm comparisons are underpowered within subtype, so this reads as support for biomarker-directed ADT rather than a rule for omission.

studies.interpretation:
The question worth asking of any biomarker analysis from a salvage RT trial is whether it is prognostic, predictive, or both, because only the predictive claim changes what gets prescribed. A prognostic marker tells you who does badly; a predictive one tells you whose outcome moves with treatment. The tweet asserts both for PAM50 Luminal B, and the evidence offered for the predictive half is a formal interaction test on FFP (P=0.01) plus a second on 10-y MFS (p-int=.05). That is the right kind of evidence. It is also the kind that is easiest to overread.

Start with what the comparison actually is. The FFP slide pools the two STADT-containing arms against PBRT alone, which means the contrast confounds ADT with pelvic nodal RT in half of the treated group. The three-arm slide partly untangles this: within one subtype panel, Arm 2 vs 1 is HR 0.63 (0.35-1.10) and Arm 3 vs 2 is HR 0.64 (0.34-1.20), neither clearing conventional thresholds, while the full escalation from Arm 1 to Arm 3 does (p=0.004). Read plainly, the within-subtype data cannot say whether the benefit belongs to ADT, to nodal coverage, or to the two together. The headline that Luminal B predicts ADT benefit is therefore a statement about the pooled contrast, and a reader deciding on pelvic volume gets nothing firm here.

The second issue is who was analysed. The cohort is 709 of 1792 enrolled and evaluable men, filtered by consent, tissue availability and two assay QC steps. Nothing in the source compares these men to those who dropped out. If tissue quality tracks era, institution or specimen size, the analytic cohort may not carry the parent trial's randomisation balance within subtype, and an interaction test is only as trustworthy as that balance.

Third, the strength of the two interactions differs. FFP is largely a PSA-driven endpoint, and ADT suppresses PSA directly, so a larger FFP effect in a hormonally driven subtype is the expected finding and the least persuasive one. MFS is the endpoint that would carry the argument, and there the interaction is at the margin (p-int=.05) with the non-Luminal B estimate reported as -3%, a number whose sign says more about noise than about harm.

How this sits against existing practice: ADT with salvage RT is currently chosen on PSA level, grade and margin status, and trials such as GETUG-AFU 16 and RADICALS-HD tested it without molecular selection. NRG GU006 took the PAM50 hypothesis forward prospectively with salvage RT. This analysis is consistent with that direction and adds a larger randomised dataset with longer horizons, but it does not by itself license withholding ADT from non-Luminal B men. That would need an estimate in that group tight enough to exclude a clinically relevant benefit, and the source shows only a garbled HR with an upper bound at 1.00.

It would be wrong if the subtype effect disappears after adjustment for PSA at entry, or if it fails to replicate in an independent trial cohort.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Open-label randomized phase III**, 1:1, **298 randomized** at 27 centers (16/12/2013 to 20/03/2017), 296 evaluable: 141 brachytherapy boost, 155 EBRT. Median PFS follow-up **61.7 months** (55.5-62.8).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Intermediate-risk prostate cancer**: PSA 10 to 20 ng/ml and/or Gleason 7 and/or T2b; age 18-80, ECOG PS ≤ 2, expected survival ≥ 10y. **Excluded: ADT**, T3a, nodal or distant disease, IPSS >15, active inflammatory bowel disease. Median age 69; 60.5% Gleason 3+4, 27% 4+3, 12.5% Gleason 6; mean PSA 8.90.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Both arms: **EBRT 46 Gy at 2 Gy/fraction** to prostate + first cm of seminal vesicles. **Arm A:** brachytherapy boost to prostate, I-125 permanent implant **110 Gy** or Ir-192 HDR **14 Gy**, technique chosen by center (79 LDR, 55 HDR, 7 unknown). **Arm B:** EBRT boost 34 Gy at 2 Gy/fraction to prostate only, **total 80 Gy**.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** PSA-PFS at 5 years by Phoenix criteria. **Secondary:** OS, PCSS, MFS, adverse events, QoL (IPSS, IIEF-5, QLQ-C30). PCSS and MFS results not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: 5-yr PSA-PFS **87.8% vs 88.8%** (brachy vs EBRT, p=0.86) on 35 events; 5-yr OS 96.0% vs 92.7% (p=0.30). **No benefit in either the 3+4 or 4+3 subgroup**, and LDR vs HDR did not influence PSA-PFS.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Abstract: more acute and late urinary toxicity with brachy boost (**55% vs 26%**, p<0.0001; **82% vs 64%**, p=0.0007), mostly grade 1-2 (pollakiuria, dysuria), **no difference in grade 3**, no grade 4. The slide's acute GU all-grade rates (79.3% vs 79.7%, p=0.92) and its acute GI difference (29.9% vs 41.2%, p=0.03) do not match the abstract text.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: ASCENDE-RT is the randomized trial that established a biochemical control advantage for an LDR boost over dose-escalated EBRT, in a higher-risk cohort that all received ADT. GETUG P05 asks the same question in **intermediate-risk disease without ADT** and finds **no PSA-PFS difference**.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents intermediate-risk prostate cancer (mostly Gleason 3+4, mean PSA 8.90) treated with conventionally fractionated RT and no ADT. Does not represent T3a or node-positive disease, pts receiving ADT, or baseline IPSS >15.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: **35 events** leaves room for a modest difference either way, and the source states neither the hypothesized effect nor power. Two boost techniques at center discretion make the experimental arm heterogeneous. Toxicity figures differ between the abstract and the presented slide.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: For intermediate-risk disease without ADT, 80 Gy EBRT matched a brachytherapy boost on 5-yr biochemical control with less late GU toxicity. It does not settle whether curves separate later, or whether a boost adds value in unfavorable intermediate-risk disease managed with ADT.

studies.interpretation:
GETUG P05 tests the brachytherapy dose-escalation hypothesis in a clean form: no ADT in either arm, an identical 46 Gy first phase to the prostate and proximal seminal vesicles, and a control boost that takes the prostate to 80 Gy. A null result on biochemical control sits awkwardly beside ASCENDE-RT, which found better biochemical control with an LDR boost than with dose-escalated EBRT. The two are not the same experiment, though. ASCENDE-RT enrolled a higher-risk mix and gave ADT and pelvic nodal RT to everyone, whereas this trial enrolled intermediate-risk disease only and excluded ADT. The simplest reconciliation is that the marginal value of further intraprostatic dose depends on baseline risk, and that this cohort started close to the ceiling.

The baseline data support that reading. 12.5% had Gleason 6 disease, 60.5% were Gleason 3+4, and mean PSA was 8.90, so a large share would be called favorable intermediate-risk today. With both arms near 88% PSA-PFS at 5 years and only 35 events among 296 evaluable pts, the trial can argue against a large boost effect but cannot exclude a modest one. The source gives neither the difference the trial was designed to detect nor its power, so how firmly the null should be held is unknown.

Timing matters as well. PSA failures in intermediate-risk disease treated without ADT accrue slowly, and a median follow-up of 61.7 months may precede any separation. The Phoenix definition also behaves differently after an implant, where benign PSA bounces can register as events, which would bias against the boost arm if anything. Neither point rescues the experimental arm, but both argue for waiting on longer follow-up and on the MFS secondary endpoint, which the source lists but does not report.

The experimental arm was not one intervention. Centers chose between an I-125 implant at 110 Gy and Ir-192 HDR at 14 Gy, and whether those are equivalent escalations is debatable. The abstract reports no influence of technique on PSA-PFS, but subgroups of 79 and 55 pts sharing a handful of events cannot answer that. Spreading accrual over 27 centers also raises the usual implant-quality question, and no dosimetric quality data appear in the source.

On toxicity the direction is consistent, the details are not. Late GU events were more frequent with the boost (82.2% vs 63.6% on the slide), with grade 2 at 34.1% vs 17.9% and grade 3 uncommon in both arms. The abstract's acute urinary figures (55% vs 26%) do not match the slide's acute GU all-grade rates (79.3% vs 79.7%), and the slide's acute GI difference contradicts the abstract's statement of no GI difference. Until a manuscript resolves this, the toxicity comparison is provisional, and the reported absence of a QoL or sexual function difference tempers it.

What changes is narrow. For intermediate-risk prostate cancer managed without ADT, dose-escalated conventional EBRT is defensible without an implant. The trial says nothing about high-risk disease, boost combined with ADT, brachytherapy monotherapy, or moderately hypofractionated and SBRT comparators.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The boost decision is the read: an LDR 110 Gy or HDR 14 Gy boost after 46 Gy gave the same 5-yr PSA-PFS as EBRT to 80 Gy at 2 Gy/fraction, with late GU toxicity 82.2% vs 63.6% (p=0.0006). Applies to intermediate-risk disease without ADT; hypofractionated and SBRT comparators were not tested.

Brachy boost value in unfavorable intermediate-risk disease treated with ADT

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Biomarker evaluation in **two prospective post-op SBRT cohorts** (SCIMITAR, EXCALIBUR). Risk scores came from the **original intact-prostate model** without refitting. Discrimination assessed as continuous AUC and as dichotomized performance at the prespecified **0.50** threshold, then exploratory threshold recalibration; AUCs bootstrapped (1,000 iterations) and pooled by fixed-effects meta-analysis.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Post-prostatectomy pts receiving SBRT to the prostate fossa. **SCIMITAR:** 100 enrolled, **89 evaluable**. **EXCALIBUR:** **74 evaluable**. Adjuvant vs salvage mix, PSA at RT and ADT use not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: SCIMITAR: **30-34 Gy in 5 fractions** to the prostate fossa **± pelvic nodes**. EXCALIBUR: 5-fraction SBRT to the prostate bed ± nodes, dose not reported in source. Toxicity by nodal coverage not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Outcome:** late grade 2+ GU adverse events. Predictor: PROSTOX Ultra score, continuous and dichotomized. Toxicity scale and follow-up duration not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Per-cohort discrimination is in the table. **Pooled AUC at 0.25 was 0.748**. Clinical covariates (age, baseline pad use, IPSS, time from RP to SBRT) were **not associated** with toxicity (all p>0.2).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The signature was built and thresholded for late GU AEs after **intact-prostate SBRT**, where 0.50 was prespecified. Post-op, risk ordering held (continuous AUC 0.814 and 0.824) but the **0.50 cutoff did not transfer**: EXCALIBUR binary AUC was <0.50.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents post-prostatectomy pts treated with 5-fraction SBRT to the prostate fossa ± pelvic nodes. Does not represent conventionally fractionated or moderately hypofractionated post-op RT, or intact-prostate SBRT, where the 0.50 threshold was set.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: **Sensitivity and specificity at 0.25 are not reported** in the source text, only AUC. EXCALIBUR's event count and both cohorts' follow-up duration are missing, so the stability of the EXCALIBUR estimates cannot be judged. Source is a trade-press account of a talk, not a full report.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The read is a **stable germline signal with a downward-shifted trigger** after prostatectomy. That supports the biology and leaves the clinical tool unfinished: a cutoff tuned on these cohorts needs an independent post-op set before it gates fractionation or counseling.

studies.interpretation:
The interesting result here is a dissociation. Ranked as a continuous score, the signature separates men who develop late grade 2+ GU toxicity from those who do not about equally well in both cohorts (AUC 0.814 and 0.824), and the score distributions sit far apart (medians 0.547 vs 0.049 in SCIMITAR, 0.338 vs 0.043 in EXCALIBUR). Applied as the binary test it was built to be, at the 0.50 threshold prespecified for intact-prostate SBRT, it fails in one of the two cohorts: EXCALIBUR's dichotomized AUC fell below 0.50, and the figure annotation says every pt with toxicity there scored under the cutoff. A test that is highly specific (0.926 and 0.985) and misses that many events is a rule-in tool at best, and in a post-op population it would hand low-risk labels to the men it was meant to flag.

The investigators' explanation, that genetic risk ordering persists while the dose-response context changes after prostatectomy, is plausible on its face. The fossa is a different target than an intact gland, the bladder neck and anastomosis sit in the high-dose volume, and baseline urinary function has already been altered by surgery. A fixed germline susceptibility could reasonably translate to toxicity at a lower score. But plausibility is carrying weight the data cannot yet carry. The 0.25 threshold was selected from a candidate range of roughly 0.10 to 0.31 by searching these same two cohorts for a cutoff meeting sensitivity and specificity floors, and the reported AUCs at 0.25 (0.727, 0.750, pooled 0.748) are scored on the data that chose it. That is an optimistic estimate by construction. The source also gives AUC at 0.25 without the sensitivity and specificity that a clinician would actually use, and a binary AUC around 0.75 leaves real room for either to be mediocre.

Two further gaps limit how far the finding travels. The cohorts differ in ways the source does not resolve: SCIMITAR's dose is given as 30 to 34 Gy in 5 fractions, EXCALIBUR's is not stated, both allowed pelvic nodal treatment, and there is no breakdown of toxicity by dose level or nodal coverage. If the median score among men with toxicity differs between cohorts (0.547 vs 0.338) partly because of technique, then a single post-op cutoff may itself be context-dependent. And the absence of association for age, pad use, IPSS and surgery-to-RT interval (all p>0.2) is reassuring for the signature's independence but is a null finding in modest cohorts, not evidence those factors are irrelevant.

What this changes is narrow and worth stating precisely. It does not validate a post-op test. It does show that the intact-prostate threshold should not be carried over to fossa SBRT, and it gives a specific, falsifiable cutoff to test prospectively. Whether a high score should move a man toward conventional fractionation, a lower dose, or smaller volumes is untested here: neither cohort assigned treatment by score, and no conventionally fractionated post-op group was examined.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The cutoff, not the signature, is what breaks post-op: in EXCALIBUR every pt with toxicity scored below 0.50, and the median score with toxicity was 0.338. Read against the intact-prostate threshold, a score can look low-risk before late G2+ GU toxicity after 5-fx fossa SBRT (30-34 Gy in SCIMITAR).

open_questions: Independent prospective validation of the 0.25 post-op threshold
Does a high score warrant conventional fractionation, lower dose, or smaller volume?
Does the signature predict late GU toxicity after conventionally fractionated post-op RT?

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Systematic review (183 articles) plus 3-round modified Delphi**, May 2025 to February 2026. **48 experts from 15 countries**: 34 radiation oncologists, 7 medical oncologists, 7 urologic oncologists. **Consensus = ≥75% agreement**; independently peer reviewed, endorsed by ASTRO and ESTRO.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Men with GU adverse events associated with prostate cancer RT, split by **intact prostate vs postoperative** and, when intact, **obstructive vs irritative** predominance. Five domains: acute medical management, RT technique, bladder outlet obstruction, urology referral indications, hyperbaric oxygen. Recommendations assume UTI has been excluded.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **76% favored moderate hypofractionation over SBRT at baseline IPSS 15–19**; **85%** recommended a full bladder at simulation and treatment. After a bladder outlet procedure, **94% would wait ≥8 weeks** and 66% ≥12 weeks before RT; only **52%** considered SBRT safe afterward. **No dose-volume constraint reached consensus.**

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Agreement figures and IPSS threshold distributions are tabulated in the bullets. The manuscript reports consensus on **31 key questions**; the source covers a subset.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The presenter cited MIRAGE for margin reduction (**2-mm MRI-guided vs 4-mm CT-guided, late G≥2 GU 51% → 27%**) and CHHiP, PROFIT, RTOG 0415 and the HYDRA meta-analysis as showing no consistent late GU increase with moderate hypofractionation. RICH-ART was cited as randomized support for hyperbaric oxygen in late radiation cystitis; no effect size reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents men receiving prostate cancer RT, intact prostate or post-prostatectomy, with acute or late GU adverse events. Does not represent non-radiation populations such as BPH or overactive bladder, from which management was previously extrapolated.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Several quoted positions fall **below the group's own ≥75% bar** (74%, 74%, 66%, 52%). The source gives **60% for IPSS ≥15** and 61% for the 15–19 band without reconciling them. Outlet-procedure questions were voted by a panel with 34 radiation oncologists and 7 urologic oncologists.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: A default sequence for symptom management and an IPSS-anchored fractionation preference now exist where practice was improvised. Still unsettled, per the working group: **dose-volume constraints, reliability of urethral contouring, and RT-specific evidence for commonly used medications**. Four ongoing trials are named (BEFORE, RadTARGET, RELIEF, DESTINATION-2) and the document is intended to be living.

studies.interpretation:
What this document offers is structure where practice has been improvised, and its value should be judged on that basis rather than as evidence of efficacy. Every percentage in it is the share of a panel holding an opinion. None is an outcome, so a 94% agreement to wait at least 8 weeks after an outlet procedure tells a reader how uniform expert habit is, not how much toxicity the wait prevents. The source concedes the gap: management has been borrowed from BPH and overactive bladder populations, and the working group lists RT-specific evidence for commonly used medications among the things still missing.

The RT-technique domain deserves the closest reading, because it is where opinion and the cited data pull in different directions. The panel leaned toward moderate hypofractionation over SBRT at baseline IPSS 15–19, and the presentation paired that with CHHiP, PROFIT, RTOG 0415 and the HYDRA meta-analysis as not showing a consistent rise in late GU events with moderate hypofractionation. That supports moderate hypofractionation as tolerable. It does not show that SBRT is worse at that symptom burden, and the report cites no randomized comparison of the two schedules stratified by baseline IPSS. The one SBRT trial named, MIRAGE, points somewhere else: margin and image guidance, not fraction number, as the modifiable variable. A reader with MR guidance and 2-mm margins could reasonably ask whether the IPSS threshold was set with CT-guided, wider-margin SBRT in mind. The source does not say.

Confidence should also track the consensus rule the group set for itself. The threshold was ≥75%, and several of the most quotable positions sit under it: 74% on alpha blockers lacking benefit after prostatectomy, 74% on referral at IPSS ≥20, 66% on a 12-week wait, 52% on SBRT being safe after an outlet procedure. Those are majority views, and the last is close to an even split. The inconsistency on the fractionation threshold (60% for IPSS ≥15 in one sentence, 61% for the 15–19 band in the next) suggests a secondhand conference report is not a reliable substitute for the manuscript's own tables.

Panel composition matters for the procedural questions. Of 48 panelists, 34 were radiation oncologists and 7 were urologic oncologists, so positions on when a urologist should operate were largely voted by the referring specialty. That does not make them wrong, but the outlet-procedure thresholds would carry more weight with urology-led data behind them.

What would change the read: prospective dose-volume or urethral-sparing data, which the group names as absent, and results from the four ongoing trials it lists. Until then this is a defensible default sequence for symptom management and a map of where the field has no data, most pointedly the absence of any agreed dose-volume constraint.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Fractionation choice now has an IPSS anchor: 76% favored moderate hypofractionation over SBRT at baseline IPSS 15–19, and 85% a full bladder at simulation and treatment. No dose-volume constraint reached consensus, and only 52% considered SBRT safe after a bladder outlet procedure, with 94% waiting ≥8 weeks before RT.

Reliability of urethral contouring
RT-specific evidence for commonly used GU symptom medications

📊 Local failure lower with STAD despite dose escalation: HR 0.44, p<0.001

With 88% treated by EBRT alone to 79.2 Gy, the trial cannot say whether a brachytherapy boost substitutes for ADT. 422 of 446 deaths were non-prostate, which is why OS stayed flat.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Phase III prospective randomized trial**, accrued 1538 pts 2009-2016, **1493 eligible for analysis** (751 RT alone, 742 RT + STAD). Stratified by number of risk factors (1 vs 2-3), ACE-27 (≥2 vs <2), and RT modality. Median follow-up **9.4 years** (10.3 years in survivors).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Non-metastatic **intermediate-risk prostate cancer** with ≥1 of: clinical stage T2b-T2c, Gleason score 7, PSA >10 but ≤20 ng/mL. **Ineligible: all 3 risk factors with ≥50% positive cores.** Median age 68, 67% single risk factor, 92% Gleason 7, median PSA 8.1 ng/mL, 67% ACE-27 <2.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: **STAD:** LHRH agonist/antagonist plus oral antiandrogen for **6 months**, added to dose-escalated RT. Protocol-compliant or acceptable variation in 91% for the LHRH component and 87% for the antiandrogen.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Physician's choice of **EBRT alone to 79.2 Gy** or **EBRT 45 Gy plus LDR or HDR brachytherapy boost**. EBRT alone in 88% (abstract) to 89% (slide). Over 90% of RT plans scored per protocol or variation acceptable for contours and dose.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** overall survival, powered to detect 5-year OS 90% to 93% (HR 0.66) with 85% power. **Secondary:** biochemical failure, local failure, distant metastasis, prostate cancer death, initiation of salvage therapy, non-prostate cancer death.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **Primary OS not met** (HR 0.87, p=0.13). Every disease-control secondary favored STAD, including **local failure HR 0.44** (per-arm local failure rates not reported in source).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Overall late grade ≥3 AEs **did not differ** (HR 1.08, 95% CI 0.84-1.40). With STAD: grade ≥3 metabolic/lab **20 vs 4**, grade 3 sexual function **71 vs 38**, grade ≥3 cardiac **26 vs 10** (each p<0.01). EPIC hormone and sexual domains dropped early with STAD and largely converged by 60 months; urinary and bowel domains were similar.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The case for short-term ADT in intermediate-risk disease was built by RTOG 9408 and the D'Amico Dana-Farber trial with conventional-dose RT, leaving open whether dose escalation would erase the benefit. This trial tests that directly and finds the disease-control benefit **persists with dose-escalated RT**, in line with EORTC 22991.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents non-metastatic intermediate-risk prostate cancer treated mostly with EBRT alone to 79.2 Gy, two-thirds with a single risk factor. Does not represent pts with all 3 risk factors and ≥50% positive cores, and has limited data for brachytherapy-boost pts.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Disease-control gains are **secondary endpoints**, and the source states no multiplicity adjustment. MFS (p=0.042) is driven mostly by deaths, with only 40 vs 14 distant metastasis events. Brachytherapy-boost strata are small, and subgroup HRs for OS and MFS are not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: STAD buys fewer PSA failures, fewer metastases, less salvage ADT and fewer prostate cancer deaths, **not a demonstrated survival gain**, in a cohort where 422 of 446 deaths were non-prostate. The investigators could not identify a subgroup without benefit for PSA failure and distant metastasis, so omission still rests on competing risk and toxicity tolerance rather than trial-defined selection.

studies.interpretation:
The trial was built around a survival hypothesis that looks optimistic in hindsight. It was powered to detect a 5-year OS improvement from 90% to 93% (HR 0.66) and delivered HR 0.87 with a confidence interval of 0.72-1.04. That is not evidence of no effect. It is a trial that cannot separate a modest survival benefit from none. The cause-of-death split explains why: 422 of the 446 deaths were from causes other than prostate cancer, in men with a median age of 68 at entry. When the disease accounts for so small a share of mortality, even a large relative reduction in prostate cancer death (19 vs 5 deaths, HR 0.26) barely moves the all-cause curve.

What the result does settle is the question that motivated the design for radiation oncologists: whether dose escalation makes short-term ADT redundant. The earlier randomized support for short-term ADT in this risk group, RTOG 9408 and the Dana-Farber trial led by D'Amico, came from the conventional-dose era, and a common inference was that the hormonal benefit partly compensated for inadequate local dose. Here, with EBRT to 79.2 Gy or a brachytherapy boost, local failure was still lower with STAD (HR 0.44), as were PSA failure and distant metastasis. The compensation hypothesis does not survive that. ADT is doing something that dose alone does not.

Several features should temper how much weight the secondary endpoints carry. They are secondary, there are many of them, and the source describes no multiplicity control. The MFS result (HR 0.83, p=0.042) sits close to the threshold and is largely an echo of the OS curve: 14-year MFS of 50% vs 57% tracks 14-year OS of 53% vs 58%, with only 40 vs 14 metastatic events contributing. The prostate cancer-specific mortality estimates are 2.7% vs 0.4% at 10 years and 3.3% vs 2.1% at 14 years, and the late estimates rest on few men at risk. Whether STAD prevents prostate cancer death or defers it is not something this dataset can answer.

Generalization has clear edges. EBRT alone was used in 88%, so the brachytherapy-boost strata are too small to show whether a boost changes the STAD benefit. Two-thirds had a single risk factor, and men with all three risk factors and at least 50% positive cores were excluded, so the population leans toward the lower end of intermediate risk. The PSA-failure HR was 0.66 with one risk factor and 0.52 with two or three, a consistent relative effect, but the source gives no absolute rates by subgroup, and absolute benefit is what an omission decision turns on.

The decision the trial informs is a trade, not a mandate. Overall late grade 3 or higher toxicity was similar (HR 1.08), yet cardiac events (26 vs 10), metabolic events (20 vs 4) and grade 3 sexual dysfunction (71 vs 38) were more frequent with STAD. Non-prostate cancer mortality was not higher (HR 0.93), which argues against the cardiac signal translating into deaths, and EPIC hormone and sexual domains largely converged by 60 months. Against that sits a halving of later salvage ADT (15% vs 7% at 14 years). The reading would change if genomic classifiers, MMAI or advanced imaging can identify men whose baseline risk is too low for the relative effect to matter, which the investigators flag as unresolved.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Dose escalation did not make STAD redundant: local failure still fell (HR 0.44) and the PSA-failure benefit held in single-risk-factor pts (HR 0.66). With 88% treated by EBRT alone to 79.2 Gy, the trial cannot say whether a brachytherapy boost substitutes for ADT.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Six months of LHRH agonist/antagonist plus antiandrogen roughly halved later salvage ADT (15% vs 7% at 14 y) and cut distant metastasis (40 vs 14 events) without an OS gain. The cost is more grade ≥3 cardiac (26 vs 10) and metabolic (20 vs 4) events, though non-prostate mortality was not higher (HR 0.93).

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Trade-press write-up of a single ASTRO 2026 talk (Spratt) covering the **POSEIDON IPD meta-analysis** (6 randomized trials, 6,057 pts, median f/u 9.0 years), an adverse-feature IPD meta-analysis, **NRG GU006 (BALANCE)**, retrospective PAM50 work in RTOG 0534, and an MMAI digital pathology biomarker in NRG/RTOG 9601 and 0534.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: NRG GU006: post-radical prostatectomy, **PSA 0.1-1.0 ng/mL, N0M0**, PAM50 subtyped before randomization. RTOG 0534: post-radical prostatectomy, PSA 0.1-2.0 ng/mL, N0M0.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: GU006: blinded 1:1 randomization to salvage RT + **6 months of apalutamide** vs RT + 6 months of placebo. RTOG 0534 arms included RT alone and RT with 6 months of ADT. POSEIDON compared short-term ADT of 4-6 months with long-term ADT of 24 months.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: RT dose, fractionation and target volume for the reported trials are **not stated in source**. The planned SYMPHONY program tests the RT questions directly: 5-fraction vs conventional 20-33 fraction prostate bed SBRT, reduced vs normal dose, and added elective nodal RT.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Effect sizes are in the tables above. The pattern across datasets: hormone therapy benefit tracks **pre-RT PSA above 0.50 ng/mL** and **PAM50 luminal B**, and does not track adverse pathologic feature count.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The talk frames PAM50 against Decipher, which the speaker's figure places at **Simon level 1B** via prospective-retrospective validation in randomized cohorts including RTOG 9601 and RTOG 0534. PAM50 is presented as a step past that, a **level 1A predictive biomarker**, because NRG GU006 stratified on it prospectively.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents men after radical prostatectomy with PSA 0.1-1.0 ng/mL and N0M0 disease being considered for salvage RT. Does not represent N+/M+ recurrence, which the planned SYMPHONY-FULL-SCORE addresses.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The RTOG 0534 PAM50 analysis is **post-hoc** and only one of three luminal B comparisons reached p = 0.004; the other two were p=0.10 and p = 0.16. MMAI figures are approximate curve reads. The write-up does not say how N0M0 was staged.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The case for intensification in luminal B is better supported than the case for omission in non-luminal B: the non-luminal B MFS estimate (HR 1.06, 95% CI 0.41-2.78) cannot exclude either benefit or harm. GU006 tested apalutamide, so it does not by itself answer whether PAM50 selects for ADT.

studies.interpretation:
The talk's argument is that clinical variables sort prognosis but not treatment effect, and that a predictive biomarker is what the hormone therapy decision with post-operative RT has been missing. POSEIDON is the foundation. Across 6 randomized trials and 6,057 pts, adding hormone therapy gave an OS HR of 0.87 with a CI reaching 1.01, and 24 months did no better than 4-6 months (HR 0.96). Read flat, that argues against routine ADT. The PSA-stratified analysis is why the flat read is wrong: the benefit sits above a pre-RT PSA of 0.50 ng/mL (HR 0.72 and 0.69), and at PSA ≤0.20 the point estimate is on the wrong side of 1 (HR 1.14).

That creates a practical tension. Salvage RT has been moving toward lower PSA, which is the stratum where the pooled data show no OS gain from hormone therapy. PSA as a selector therefore loses discriminating power as practice shifts earlier, and the obvious fallback, adverse pathology, does not fill the gap. Adverse feature count was prognostic (OS HR 1.25 per feature) but the interaction with hormone therapy was null for OS (p = 0.40). The MFS interaction deserves a more careful read than the slide's summary gives it: HR 0.88 with a CI of 0.77-1.01 and p = 0.08 is a failure to demonstrate an interaction, not a demonstration that none exists.

PAM50 is offered as the answer, and NRG GU006 is the only prospectively biomarker-stratified piece of the evidence. In luminal B, 5-year bPFS was 72% vs 54% and MFS 95% vs 82%. The MFS HR of 0.27 carries a CI of 0.07-0.95, which implies few events and an upper bound close to 1. The non-luminal B bPFS estimate is reported with an 80% CI while everything else uses 95%, and the write-up does not explain why, so the underlying statistical design cannot be judged from this source. Two further points limit how far the result travels. The experimental agent was apalutamide, so GU006 shows that luminal B identifies benefit from 6 months of apalutamide with salvage RT, whereas the RTOG 0534 analysis concerns ADT; the two are complementary, not the same intervention. And the RTOG 0534 analysis is post-hoc, its endpoint and arm comparisons are not named in the write-up, and only one of three luminal B comparisons (HR 0.40, p = 0.004) reached nominal significance.

The asymmetry matters for de-escalation. Withholding systemic therapy in non-luminal B rests on an MFS HR of 1.06 with a CI of 0.41-2.78, which is compatible with meaningful benefit or harm. The data support adding in luminal B more firmly than omitting elsewhere.

The MMAI material is a weaker tier. The speaker acknowledged it went from training to randomized-trial validation without a standalone independent validation step, the figures quoted (approximately 40% vs 20% at 12 years in MMAI-high) are approximate, and no interaction test is reported. None of this touches RT dose, fractionation or nodal coverage, which SYMPHONY is designed to address. This is also one speaker's synthesis relayed secondhand, from an investigator whose own work (Spratt DE et al, JCO 2017 and JCO 2018) built the Decipher validation pathway shown.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Pre-RT PSA, not pathology, sorted hormone therapy benefit in POSEIDON: OS HR 1.14 at PSA ≤0.20 ng/mL vs 0.72 at 0.51-1.0 and 0.69 above 1.0, while adverse feature count showed no interaction (p = 0.40). That weakens GG4-5 or SVI alone as the reason to add ADT to early salvage RT.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: The systemic read is agent and duration: 24 months of ADT did not beat 4-6 months for OS (HR 0.96), and NRG GU006 tested 6 months of apalutamide, not ADT. Luminal B selected for benefit (5-year MFS 95% vs 82%); non-luminal B did not (90% vs 89%).

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Cross-trial IPD comparison** of LUNAR and SATURN, **n=63**, with an **IPTW-adjusted** primary comparison of RLT vs AAT. Not a randomised comparison between the two systemic partners. Median follow-up not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **M1 oligorecurrent PCa post-RP**. Prior hormone therapy and prior MDT were both permitted, since each appears as a yes/no covariate in the model. Lesion number, imaging modality and other eligibility detail not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: **SBRT + 177Lu-PNT2002 RLT** (LUNAR, n=20) vs **SBRT + 6 mo androgen annihilation therapy** (SATURN, n=25), with an **SBRT alone** group (n=18). RLT activity, cycle number and AAT drug components not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Eugonadal progression-free survival (euPFS)**, reported as median time to progression and progression rate per group, plus an IPTW-weighted multivariable Cox model. The euPFS event definition is not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: RLT vs AAT adjusted **HR 1.39 (95% CI 0.56-3.45), p=0.47**. **PSADT** was independently associated with euPFS, **HR 0.87 per month (95% CI 0.77-0.98; p=0.018)**, with no PSADT difference among groups.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Grade ≥3 AEs **10% (2) with RLT vs 20% (5) with AAT, p=0.357**. RLT events were lymphopenia, 2 (10%). AAT events were rash / hypertension 4 (16%) and hepatic toxicity 1 (4%).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: ORIOLE and STOMP tested MDT against observation in oligometastatic PCa, and EXTEND and RADIOSA tested adding hormone therapy to MDT. This analysis asks the next question, whether a radioligand can stand in for the hormonal partner, without a randomised answer.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents M1 oligorecurrent PCa post-RP treated with SBRT plus either 177Lu-PNT2002 or 6 mo AAT. Does not represent pts without prior RP or disease beyond the oligorecurrent state.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: **SBRT dose, fractionation and target volume are not reported**, so RT comparability across the two trials cannot be checked. The euPFS definition, follow-up and staging imaging are also absent, and the KM p < 0.0001 is not tied to a named comparison.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The clear separation is SBRT alone vs either intensified group, not RLT vs AAT. The RLT vs AAT estimate is **uninformative on equivalence**. The PSADT association is prognostic only: no treatment-by-PSADT interaction is reported in source.

studies.interpretation:
The contrast that looks decisive here is the least informative one. SBRT alone against either intensified group is the easy comparison: all 18 SBRT-alone pts progressed, at a median of 6.0 mo, while the two combination groups sat at 19.4 and 21.7 mo. That MDT by itself buys limited time in oligorecurrent prostate cancer is the premise ORIOLE and STOMP left the field with, and the reason EXTEND and RADIOSA went on to test hormone therapy alongside MDT. Seeing it again in a small pooled dataset adds little.

The question worth the reader's attention is the one between the two partners, and there the data cannot carry the word "similar". The adjusted estimate is HR 1.39 with a 95% CI of 0.56-3.45, built on 12 events among 20 RLT pts and 17 among 25 AAT pts. An interval that wide is compatible with the radioligand being clearly better and with it being several-fold worse. No non-inferiority margin appears in the source, so p=0.47 is an absence of evidence, not a finding of equivalence.

The cross-trial structure compounds this. IPTW can balance what was measured, and the forest plot shows the covariates that went in: PSADT, baseline PSA, age, prior hormone therapy, prior MDT. It cannot balance what differs between two protocols by design. The source gives no SBRT dose, fractionation or target volume for either trial, no staging modality, no lesion count, and no surveillance schedule. Any of these could shift time to progression by more than the difference between 19.4 and 21.7 mo. For an RT reader, the missing technique parameters are the main obstacle: without them there is no way to confirm the radiation component was held constant, which is the assumption the whole comparison rests on.

The endpoint deserves a second look as well. Eugonadal PFS is a reasonable way to avoid crediting an ADT-containing arm for time spent castrate, but the source does not define the event or say how the clock was handled in a group that never received hormonal suppression. A comparison between a testosterone-suppressing regimen and a non-suppressing one is sensitive to exactly that definition.

The PSADT result is probably the most durable observation. Each additional month of PSADT was associated with a 13% reduction in euPFS event risk (HR 0.87 per month, p=0.018), and the groups did not differ on PSADT. That points to disease kinetics, not the choice of partner, as the dominant driver in this dataset. It is a prognostic association only: no interaction test is reported, so it does not show that slow-PSADT pts can be managed with SBRT alone.

On toxicity, grade ≥3 events were 10% (2) with RLT and 20% (5) with AAT, p=0.357, and the event types differ in kind between the two. The counts are too small to rank the regimens. What this analysis supports is a randomised trial of SBRT plus radioligand against SBRT plus short-course hormonal therapy. It leaves the current choice of systemic partner where it was.

Grade ≥3 AEs were 10% (2) vs 20% (5), p=0.357, with lymphopenia on RLT and rash / hypertension and hepatic toxicity on AAT.

papers.title: Genomic Stratification of Benefit from Short-Term Androgen Deprivation with Dose-Escalated Radiotherapy in Intermediate-Risk Prostate Cancer: An Ancillary Study of NRG/RTOG 0815
papers.abstract:
ASTRO 2026 abstract 312 · SS 36 - Predicting Benefit and Toxicity: Biomarkers in Prostate Radiotherapy · 2026-09-29 · presented by Angela Jia, MD, PhD

Purpose/Objective(s): NRG/RTOG 0815 is a phase 3 randomized trial of dose-escalated radiotherapy (RT) with or without 6 months of short-term androgen deprivation therapy (STAD). We aimed to validate the potential prognostic and predictive ability of the 22-gene genomic classifier (GC) on long-term outcomes in the NRG/RTOG 0815 trial.
Materials/Methods: After National Cancer Institute approval of a prespecified analysis plan, archived prostate biopsy specimens from NRG/RTOG 0815 were profiled using a locked, clinical-grade Decipher GC assay (Veracyte, San Diego). Genomic risk was analyzed as a continuous variable and by prespecified score categories: low (GC < 0.45), intermediate (GC 0.45-0.6), and high (GC > 0.6). Linkage of GC data to updated clinical outcomes with extended follow-up was performed. The primary endpoint of this study was distant metastasis (DM). Secondary endpoints included biochemical failure (BF), metastasis-free survival (MFS), prostate cancer–specific mortality (PCSM), and overall survival (OS). Cox and Fine-Gray competing risk multivariable analysis (MVA) models adjusted for age, race, clinical risk factors, comorbidity score, and RT modality.
Results: GC scores were successfully obtained for 395 patients of 856 patients with available tissue. Baseline characteristics were balanced between arms with 10.2 years (IQR 8.4-11.4) median follow-up. There were 91 BF, 139 MFS, 16 DM, 134 OS and 7 PCSM events. On MVA, a higher GC score (int/high vs low) was independently prognostic for BF (sHR 2.19, 95% CI 1.36-3.53, p<0.001) and for DM (sHR 4.89, 95% CI 0.98-24.3, p=0.05). A significant GC-STAD interaction was observed for DM (p-interaction <0.001) and PCSM (p-interaction <0.001). Patients with low-GC scores (44% of cohort) derived no clinically meaningful benefit from STAD (10-year DM absolute difference of 1%), whereas patients with high-GC (32% of cohort) scores had a significant DM reduction with STAD (10-year DM absolute benefit of 11%).
Conclusion: In intermediate-risk prostate cancer treated with dose-escalated RT, the 22-gene GC is independently prognostic and predictive of DM benefit from STAD. Patients with low GC scores have favorable long-term outcomes with no clear benefit from treatment intensification with STAD. In contrast, patients with higher GC scores treated with RT alone had unacceptably high long-term DM rates, which were significantly improved with STAD. NRG GU010 will serve as prospective validation and build on these findings.

papers.title: Long-Term Follow-up Results for NRG/RTOG 0815: A Phase III Prospective Randomized Trial of Dose-Escalated Radiotherapy with or without Short-Term Androgen Deprivation Therapy for Patients with Intermediate-Risk Prostate Cancer
papers.abstract:
ASTRO 2026 abstract 106 · SS 02 - Escalate, De-escalate, or Substitute? Trials Shaping Prostate Cancer Care · 2026-09-27 · presented by Daniel Krauss, MD, FASTRO

Purpose/Objective(s): Initial reported results of NRG/RTOG 0815 demonstrated reductions in rates of biochemical and local failure as well as distant metastases for patients receiving short-term androgen deprivation (STAD) in addition to dose-escalated radiotherapy (RT) compared to dose-escalated RT alone. However, the study did not demonstrate a significant benefit to adding STAD with respect to overall survival. Updated clinical results with extended follow-up are presented here.
Materials/Methods: Eligible patients had intermediate risk prostate cancer defined by the presence of > 1 of the following features: clinical stage T2b-T2c, Gleason score 7, or baseline PSA > 10 and < 20 ng/mL. Patients were stratified by the presence of 1 vs. > 1 intermediate risk factor, baseline ACE-27 comorbidity score ( > 2 vs. < 2), and RT boost modality. Randomization was to dose-escalated RT alone (Arm 1) or combined with STAD consisting of LHRH agonist/antagonist plus oral anti-androgen for 6 months (Arm 2). RT was administered per the discretion of the treating physician and consisted of external beam RT (EBRT) alone to 79.2 Gy or EBRT (45 Gy) combined with LDR or HDR brachytherapy boost. The primary endpoint was overall survival.
Results: The study accrued 1538 patients between 2009-2016 with 1493 eligible for analysis, 751 on Arm 1 and 742 on Arm 2. Baseline clinical characteristics were well-balanced between treatment arms. 88% of patients were treated with dose-escalated EBRT alone, 67% had a single intermediate risk factor, and 67% an ACE-27 score < 2. Median follow-up was 9.4 years (10.3 years for surviving patients). No differences in rates of late Grade > 3 adverse events were observed between treatment arms. 446 deaths occurred, 239 in Arm 1 and 207 in Arm 2, corresponding to 14-year overall survival rates of 53% vs. 58% (HR 0.87, 95% CI: 0.72-1.04, p = 0.13). Rates of biochemical failure (HR 0.60, p < 0.001) and local failure (HR 0.44, p < 0.001) were lower in Arm 2. 40 patients developed distant metastases on Arm 1 compared to 14 on Arm 2 (HR 0.35, p < 0.001). Metastasis-free survival at 14 years was 50% for Arm 1 vs. 57% for Arm 2 (HR 0.83, p = 0.042). 19 deaths were attributed to prostate cancer on Arm 1 compared to 5 on Arm 2 (HR 0.26, p = 0.004). No significant difference in non-prostate cancer-related mortality was observed.
Conclusion: The addition of STAD to dose-escalated RT resulted in improvements in clinical failure rates, prostate cancer-specific mortality, and metastasis-free survival. No statistically significant benefit in overall survival was found.

papers.title: Brachytherapy Versus External Beam Dose-Escalated Boost for Intermediate-Risk Prostate Cancer: Definitive Results of the GETUG P05 Trial
papers.abstract:
ASTRO 2026 abstract 105 · SS 02 - Escalate, De-escalate, or Substitute? Trials Shaping Prostate Cancer Care · 2026-09-27 · presented by Ariane Lapierre, MD, PhD

Purpose/Objective(s): We evaluated external beam radiotherapy combined with a brachytherapy boost versus exclusive external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) for intermediate-risk prostate cancer.
Materials/Methods: GETUG P05 is an open-label randomized phase III trial. Patients with intermediate-risk histologically proven prostate cancer (defined as a PSA level between 10 ng/ml and 20ng/ml, and/or a Gleason score of 7 (3+4 of 4+3) and/or a T2b stage) were randomized between 2 treatment arms. Both arms received external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) delivering 46 Gy to the prostate and the first centimeter of the seminal vesicles. The treatment was then followed by a boost delivered to the prostate only, according to randomization: Arm A included a brachytherapy boost, utilizing either Iodine-125 permanent implants (110 Gy) or High-Dose-Rate (HDR) brachytherapy (Iridium-192, 14 Gy), with the choice between the two brachytherapy techniques left to the discretion of each participating center. Arm B consisted of an EBRT dose escalation boost, delivering a total dose of 80 Gy to the prostate only. Primary endpoint was PSA progression-free survival (PSA-PFS) at 5 years according to Phoenix criteria. Secondary endpoints included OS, PC-specific survival (PCSS), metastasis-free survival (MFS), adverse events (AE) and quality of life (QoL).
Results: We randomized 298 patients in 27 centers from 16/12/2013 to 20/03/2017, out of which 296 were evaluable, 155 in the EBRT arm and 141 in the brachytherapy arm (79 LDR, 55 HDR, 7 unknown). Median age was 69 (65-74); 87.5% patients had Gleason 7 (60.5% 3+4 and 27% 4+3) and 12.5% Gleason 6; initial mean PSA was 8.90 (sd=3.97). Both arms did not differ in terms of patient characteristics. Thirty-five PSA-PFS events occurred during a median PFS follow-up of 61.7 (55.5-62.8) months. Five years PSA-PFS was 87.8% in the brachytherapy arm and 88.8% in the EBRT arm (p=0.86). OS did not differ in both groups either (respectively 96.0% vs 92.7% (p=0.30)). Brachytherapy modality (I of HDR) had no influence on PSA-PFS. Quality of life and sexual function were not different in both arms. There was no benefit of brachytherapy boost in either the 3+4 or 4+3 subgroup. Regarding adverse events, the most frequent toxicities were pollakiuria and dysuria. There were statistically more acute and late urinary toxicities in the brachytherapy arm (respectively 55% vs 26% p<0.0001) and 82% vs 64% p=0.0007). However, most toxicities were grade 1 and 2 and there was no difference regarding grade 3 toxicities. There was no difference in gastrointestinal toxicities regardless of the grade and no grade 4 toxicity was observed in our study.
Conclusion: Brachytherapy boost after EBRT failed to demonstrate a benefit in PSA-PFS at 5 years. Severe toxicities and quality of life did not differ for EBRT alone or EBRT with brachytherapy boost. Clinical trials information: NCT02271659
